3. The defendant No. 2 alone contested the suit stating, inter alia, that the Insurance Company is not liable to pay the amount as the terms and conditions as stipulated in the insurance policy were not fulfilled. In defence it was also asserted that the plaintiff failed to lay any claim against the carrier for the alleged loss or damage. Further the consignor did not take proper care and caution as it appears from the survey report that the packing of the goods were inadequate and no warning label was affixed on the wooden cases which contained fragile materials namely, wired glasses. Further the suit is also bad for non-joinder of the carrier and as such the same is liable to be dismissed. 

 4. Mr. A.R. Yusuf, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, has submitted 4 grounds for our consideration. Firstly, the learned Advocate submits that the appellant has rightly avoided the claim of insurance in the present case as the same suffers for non-disclosure of material facts and utmost good faith which is an essential pre-requisite for taking a marine insurance policy. 

 8. To take up the first point of the learned Advocate for the appellant it is to be stated that a contract of Marine Insurance is a contract which is essentially based upon utmost good faith (Uberrimae fidei) and the obligation is binding upon both the contracting parties. Therefore the question necessarily arises whether the parties had the good faith at the time of taking the insurance policy as per the Bill of Lading. In the present case certain quantity of wired glasses were shipped from Karachi to be delivered at Tongi via Chittagong as per bill of lading, Ext. 2 dated 1.11.62 containing 15 wooden packages only. We find that in the bill of lading the nature of goods were specified as wired glasses which is a very fragile material. From the Bill of Lading as evidenced before the court the nature of the goods have been properly specified and both the contracting parties knew about the nature of the article and there was no lack of good faith between the parties. According to the learned Advocate, it appears from the survey report that internal packing was defective keeping sufficient room inside the packages for the movements of the wired glasses resulting in the breakage of the glasses and as such the assured ought to have disclosed this material fact to the insurer and non-disclosure of this material fact has prejudiced the insurer in fixing the premium or determining whether he will take the risk as per section 18 of the Act. We may refer here that non-disclosure of any material fact is only voidable at the option of the party prejudiced. Thus we arc called upon to see whether this non-disclosure that the internal packing was defective was such a material circumstance on the plea of which the Insurance Company could repudiate the claim under the law. Here we may refer to the insurance policy itself, Ext. 3 wherein, "the goods were declared as wired glass-sheets in wooden cases and the condition of insurance was" W.P.A., T.P.N.D., War, S.R.CC., ware-house to ware-house, including the risks of breakage and splitting subject to replacement clause." From the policy of insurance it is abundantly clear that the insurer knew about the nature of the articles and that those were packed in wooden cases. Thus this insurance policy, in the fact of the present case with the conditions attached raises a prima facie presumption that everything was done rightly between the parties. We further find from the Bill of Lading Ext. 2, that the description of goods are Foreign manufactured wired glass in 15 packages and case frail, second hand deems insufficiently packed. Therefore, the policy which was taken in the present case as per the Bill of Lading was sufficiently known to the insurer and this is really a matter wherein onus of proof lies upon the insurer to prove that the assured had failed to perform the duty of disclosure of this condition of insufficient package. In the present case P.W.1 Abdul Hye, Legal Manager of the plaintiff appeared on behalf of the plaintiff and the contesting defendant has not put a word that the plaintiff has failed to perform his part of duty in disclosing this material circumstance that the wired glasses were insufficiently packed in the wooden cases. D.W. 1 Syed Anwar Hossain, the Manager of the Insurance Company has also not stated a word in examination-in-chief that company repudiated the claim on the plea of non-disclosure of this material fact. Specific case of non-disclosure has not been made out in evidence in court by the appellant. The survey report, Ext. 1 dated 8.6.63 shows that the nature of packing was inadequate and further remarks in item 18 shows that the goods were out Aly received intact but the internal packing was equate keeping enough room for the movement of the glass with insufficient protection. From this survey report the learned Advocate for the appellant argues that if the supplier/assured packed the goods in proper condition then there would have been no loss or damage. In the facts of the present on a reference to the oral and documentary evidences as has been referred to above, we are of the view that the appellant has failed to make out a case of non-disclosure of any material fact on the part of the assured for which the insurance claim can be repudiated in the present case. A reference to section 18(3) (b) of the Act shows that the circumstance as argued by the learned Advocate for the appellant need not be disclosed as this circumstance was known to the insurer in his ordinary course of business as this was a matter of common knowledge to the insurer. Further, in view of the express warranty in the insurance policy, disclosure of this fact of insufficient packing is superfluous and redundant. The condition of insurance as contained in Ext. 3, is a condition including the risks of breakage and splitting subject to replacement clause. Thus apart from the fact that this is 401 material fact, we hold that this is also superfluous in the facts of the present case for any disclosure of such a nature. The first point raised by the learned Advocate is, therefore, not of much substance in the facts of the present case. 

 11. In this case, a reasonable notice was given and the survey was conducted on 8.5.63 and the claim was lodged with the Insurance Company on 20.5.63 by Ext. 6(f). So in the facts of the present case we find that the notice was given within time and Mr. A.R. Yusuf also does not argue this point with great force. Normally in such a claim assured is to give a notice of the loss, to furnish particulars of the loss and to furnish proof of the loss. In the present case the particulars of the loss was conveyed to the Insurance Company in due time and the proof of the same was evidenced by the survey report Ext. I. Thus in the facts of the present case the assured has proved its prima facie case of damage of the wired glasses in transit under the peril clause and the plaintiff is entitled to the relief. It is true that the surveyor was named in the insurance policy as M/s. Joseph Lobo 27, Sadarghat Road, Chittagong but in the present case the survey as conduced by another surveyor and there is nothing on record to show that the insurance company took any exception on account of this. So this condition of survey by another surveyor was accepted and by implication this condition was waived by the insurance company and the appellant also relied on this survey report to build up his case of non-disclosure. There being a loss under the policy as stipulated, we find that the defendant cannot lawfully avoid the claim of the plaintiff.
